hints: Count copper, iodine, potassium and sulfate groups on each side and look for which elements are unbalanced first.
Use the description in the stem, white precipitate in a brown solution, to decide which products are solid and which are aqueous.
walkthrough:
Balance atoms by inspection**
Start with the atoms that appear in only one compound on each side. You need 2 copper on the right to make $\text{I}_{2}$, so put 2 in front of $\text{CuSO}_{4}$ and $\text{CuI}$. That gives 2 sulfate groups on the left, so put 2 in front of $\text{K}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$. That gives 4 potassium on the right, so put 4 in front of $\text{KI}$. Now check iodine: $4$ on the left, $2 + 2 = 4$ on the right. Everything balances.

Add the correct states from the description**
Both starting chemicals are described as aqueous, so $\text{CuSO}_{4}(\text{aq})$ and $\text{KI}(\text{aq})$. $\text{CuI}$ is described as a white precipitate, so it is a solid, $\text{CuI}(\text{s})$. Iodine forms a brown solution and potassium sulfate stays dissolved, so $\text{I}_{2}(\text{aq})$ and $\text{K}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}(\text{aq})$.

hints: Remember the fixed oxidation numbers, sulfate ion is $\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$ overall and iodide ion is $\text{I}^{-}$, then work out what copper must be to balance the charge.
walkthrough:
Use the known ions to find copper**
Think of each compound as ions added together. In $\text{CuSO}_{4}$, sulfate is $\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$, so copper must be $2+$ to make a neutral compound. That means +2. In $\text{CuI}$, iodide is $\text{I}^{-}$, so copper must be $1+$ to balance it. That means +1.

Final answer: oxidation number of copper in $\text{CuSO}_{4}$ = +2
oxidation number of copper in $\text{CuI}$ = +1

hints: Compare the oxidation numbers of copper (+2 to +1) and iodine (-1 to 0) from the table and (a)(ii) to see which element increases and which decreases.
Link an increase in oxidation number to loss of electrons and a decrease to gain of electrons.
walkthrough:
Spot that both elements change**
Look at what you already know. Copper goes from +2 in $\text{CuSO}_{4}$ to +1 in $\text{CuI}$. Iodine goes from -1 in $\text{KI}$ to 0 in $\text{I}_{2}$. (Some iodide stays at -1 in $\text{CuI}$, but some is clearly oxidised to $\text{I}_{2}$.) When one species is oxidised and another is reduced in the same equation, the reaction is redox.

Translate the changes into electrons**
A fall in oxidation number means electrons have been gained, so $\text{Cu}^{2+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cu}^{+}$ is reduction. A rise in oxidation number means electrons have been lost, so $2\text{I}^{-} \rightarrow \text{I}_{2} + 2\text{e}^{-}$ is oxidation. Stating both halves clearly explains why it is redox.

Final answer: redox reaction
Iodide ions are oxidised by loss of electrons ($-1$ to $0$) AND copper(II) ions are reduced by gain of electrons (+2 to +1).

hints: Start by calculating $M_{r}$ of anhydrous $\text{CuSO}_{4}$ using $A_{r}$ values from the Data Booklet.
Use $mass = moles \times M_{r}$ to find the mass of $0.0982$ mol of $\text{CuSO}_{4}$ present in the hydrated sample.
Subtract that mass from $17.43$ g to leave the mass of water, then convert that mass to moles of $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ using $M_{r} = 18.0$.
Divide moles of $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ by moles of $\text{CuSO}_{4}$ to get the ratio $y$, then round to the nearest integer.
walkthrough:
Find $M_{r}$ of $\text{CuSO}_{4}$**
Add the $A_{r}$ values: $$M_{r}(\text{CuSO}_{4}) = 63.5 + 32.1 + (4 \times 16.0) = 159.6$$ This is the mass of one mole of anhydrous copper(II) sulfate.

Find the mass of anhydrous salt in the sample**
You are told there is $0.0982$ mol of $\text{CuSO}_{4}$ in the $17.43$ g sample: $$mass = n \times M_{r} = 0.0982 \times 159.6 = 15.67\text{ g}$$ So $15.67$ g of the $17.43$ g is $\text{CuSO}_{4}$, the rest must be water.

Convert the water mass to moles**
Mass of water: $$17.43 - 15.67 = 1.76\text{ g}$$ Moles of water with $M_{r}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O}) = 18.0$: $$n(\text{H}_{2}\text{O}) = \frac{1.76}{18.0} = 0.0978\text{ mol}$$

Find the whole number ratio $y$**
$y$ is moles of water per mole of $\text{CuSO}_{4}$: $$y = \frac{n(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})}{n(\text{CuSO}_{4})} = \frac{0.0978}{0.0982} = 0.996$$ This rounds to the integer $y = 1$, so the formula is $\text{CuSO}_{4}\cdot\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$.

Final answer: mass of $0.0982$ mol $\text{CuSO}_{4}$ = $15.67$ g
amount of $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ = $0.0978$ mol $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$
$y$ = 1
